meta.paperTitle: Döblin–Fourier cancellation and kinetic Aleksandrov estimates

summaryClaims.text: The paper develops a cancellation mechanism for kinetic equations $\partial_tu+v\cdot\nabla_xu-\mathrm{Tr}(AD_v^2u)\leq f$ with measurable uniformly elliptic coefficients, in which diffusion acts only in velocity.

Its first application is a kinetic Aleksandrov estimate, a maximum principle with the source in $L^p$, for every $p>2n+1$ when $A=A(t,v)$ and every $p>4$ when $n=1$ and $A=a(x,v)$; these thresholds are optimal among those that are uniform in the ellipticity ratios for the stated coefficient classes.

Its second application concerns position on the torus and velocity on the sphere: enhanced dissipation with the optimal square-root frequency power and, for autonomous coefficients, exponential convergence to equilibrium in weighted $L^2$ and a quantitative spectral gap.

The introduction also shows that no Fourier decay tending to zero can hold uniformly for general coefficients $A(t,x,v)$ with fixed ellipticity bounds, and conjectures how the critical exponent depends on the variables on which the coefficients depend.

ideaClaims.text: Transport along a velocity path shifts a spatial wave by the displacement accumulated along the path, so two paths whose displacements differ by half a wavelength produce waves in opposite phase.

The parabolic Harnack inequality gives the two velocity marginals a common minorant, and the corresponding contributions cancel up to a small phase error, reducing total variation by a fixed factor as in Döblin's argument.
The reduction is uniform in the starting velocity and can be repeated, and scaling determines how long each repetition takes at a given frequency, which yields exponential Fourier decay.

summaryClaims.text: For smooth $A=A(t,v)$, with constants independent of its derivatives, this section proves that for $0\leq s<t\leq1$ the Fourier transform in position of the kernel has total variation at most $C\exp(-c(t-s)\lambda^{\frac{1}{3}}\abs\xi^{\frac{2}{3}})$, where $C,c>0$ depend only on $n,\frac{\Lambda}{\lambda}$.
Scaling and iteration reduce this to a single contraction at unit frequency: over a fixed time $L$, the total variation drops from one to at most $1-\delta$, uniformly in the starting velocity.

The contraction follows two families of velocity paths whose transport produces waves with nearly opposite phases; the parabolic Harnack inequality gives their velocity marginals a common positive lower bound, and the matching portions cancel up to the small phase error.

The section also fixes the objects used later: the reflected operator $\mathcal K$, the adjoint kernel $K_{s,t}$, its velocity marginal $P$, the Dirichlet kernels $K^D$ and $P^D$, and the Fourier transform $\widehat K^\xi_{s,t}$.

ideaClaims.text: Transport turns velocity into spatial displacement, so the Fourier phase of mass records the time integral of its velocity; two velocity paths whose integrals in the direction of a unit frequency differ by $\pi$ produce opposite phases.

Because $\widehat K^\xi_{s,t}(v,\cdot)$ is a measure in the terminal velocity, the two families can cancel only where they carry mass at the same velocities; the common minorant supplies this, and the resulting fixed loss of total variation is the mechanism of Döblin's argument.

summaryClaims.text: This section proves the kinetic Aleksandrov estimate for smooth $A=A(t,v)$ on the unit cylinder, with source exponent $p>2n+1$, by estimating the solution produced by a source as the integral of the source against the kernel.

The input is an $L^q$ bound for the space-time kernel for $1<q<1+\frac{1}{2n}$, obtained by interpolating a bound for its supremum in position, from Fourier decay, with a bound for its integral in position, from the parabolic Aleksandrov estimate.
The two bounds are combined on intervals $(T,2T)$ of time elapsed since the start, and the restriction on the exponent comes from summing these contributions as $T$ tends to zero.

summaryClaims.text: For an autonomous coefficient $a(x,v)$ in dimension one, this section proves the kinetic Aleksandrov maximum principle for every source exponent $p>4$; the Bellman improvement recorded after the theorem, whose proof is in the companion manuscript, also includes $p=4$.

When $a$ depends on $x$, Fourier transformation in position no longer separates the frequencies; away from zero velocity, position is used as the time variable instead, and the resulting estimate for a velocity interval stops when velocity leaves that interval.

The difficulty is to account for later returns of velocity to the interval: velocity barriers bound them well enough for the maximum principle at $p=6$ and Hölder continuity, and a Harnack comparison derived from these gives better bounds on returns at later times, which yield every $p>4$.

The arguments are carried out for smooth $a$, with constants independent of its derivatives, and followed by an approximation; main-4 explains the steps and refers to the companion manuscript for the detailed proofs.

summaryClaims.text: This section proves the mixing theorem: it constructs the transition kernel of the spherical kinetic evolution for measurable $A$, bounds its Fourier modes, and passes from total-variation mixing to the $L^2$ bound.

Uniformly in the starting velocity, the Fourier transform of the kernel at a non-zero frequency decays at the rate $\min\{\frac{\abs\xi^2}{\lambda},\lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}\abs\xi^{\frac{1}{2}}\}$, and the power $\frac{1}{2}$ cannot be improved because of the poles of $e\cdot w$, where the phase speed is quadratic in the velocity displacement.

Summing the Fourier modes and a Döblin argument for the zero mode give mixing in total variation at rate $\min\{\lambda,\lambda^{-1}\}$; interpolation between $L^1$ and $L^\infty$ turns this into $L^2$ decay and, for autonomous $A$, a spectral gap.
The kernel comes from Krylov's construction and Markov selection; uniqueness among weak solutions is not claimed, and all estimates are uniform over the choice of evolution.

summaryClaims.text: Although the conjecture for general coefficients has been resolved, the available estimates need an exponent threshold that tends to infinity with the ellipticity ratio, whereas the sharp kinetic Aleksandrov estimate reaches thresholds valid for all ellipticity ratios.

The second reason is the cancellation mechanism itself: a contraction in total variation reminiscent of Döblin's argument, taking place in Fourier space, which captures enhanced dissipation and yields quantitative spectral-gap estimates in compact settings.

summaryClaims.text: Scaling excludes $p<2n+1$ even for constant coefficients, and nested bumps show that the estimate also fails at $p=2n+1$; the elliptic and parabolic theories show that rough coefficients may require a larger exponent; a conjecture predicts how the critical exponent depends on the variables on which the coefficients depend, around two values: $4n$, the homogeneous dimension of $(x,v)$, and $1+2n$, the scaling lower bound.

summaryClaims.text: The Aleksandrov and interior regularity estimates are first proved for smooth coefficients, with constants independent of coefficient derivatives, and then extended to measurable coefficients; the spherical evolution is treated directly for measurable coefficients.

Döblin–Fourier cancellation: two velocity paths with accumulated displacements differing by half a wavelength, each retaining some mass in a tube, receive a common velocity minorant from the parabolic Harnack inequality, and the resulting cancellation, repeated, gives exponential Fourier decay.

Both coefficient classes reduce to diffusion in some variables and transport in others, with a diffusion matrix independent of the transported variables, so that each Fourier wave in those variables evolves independently.

Aleksandrov estimate for $A(t,v)$: the parabolic estimate for the velocity marginal and Fourier decay for the spatial supremum of the kernel are interpolated on each interval $(T,2T)$ of elapsed time and summed, giving an $L^q$ kernel bound for $1<q<1+\frac{1}{2n}$ and the source range $p>2n+1$.

Aleksandrov estimate for $a(x,v)$ in dimension one: position serves as time while velocity stays away from zero, and near zero velocity a Harnack comparison controls the returning mass of narrower velocity intervals, giving every $p>4$.

Regularity: a localised cancellation argument bounds spatial derivatives, and treating $-v\cdot\nabla_xu$ as a bounded source, the parabolic Krylov–Safonov theory gives Hölder continuity in time and velocity, hence in all variables.

Mixing on the sphere: velocity paths adapted in local charts give square-root frequency decay, and parabolic Harnack on the compact sphere mixes the zero mode, which together give mixing in total variation; interpolation with the bound supplied by positivity gives weighted $L^2$ decay, and for autonomous coefficients the adjoint and a reflection of position transfer this decay to the solution semigroup and give the spectral gap.

summaryClaims.text: For a symmetric measurable coefficient matrix with $\lambda\,\mathrm{Id}_n\leq A\leq\Lambda\,\mathrm{Id}_n$, when either $A=A(t,v)$ and $p>2n+1$, or $n=1$, $A=a(x,v)$ and $p>4$, for every real-valued Borel measurable $f$, every classical sub-solution $u\in C(\overline{Q^-(P_0)})\cap C^{1,1,2}(Q^-(P_0))$ of $\mathcal Lu\leq f$ with $f_+\in L^p(Q^-(P_0))$ satisfies $\sup_{\overline{Q^-(P_0)}}u\leq\sup_{\partial_kQ^-(P_0)}u_++C_{n,\lambda,\Lambda,p}\norm{f_+}_{L^p(Q^-(P_0))}$, with a constructive constant depending only on $n,\lambda,\Lambda,p$.

By kinetic scaling the estimate holds on every cylinder $Q_R^-(P_0)$, $R>0$, with source term $C_{n,\lambda,\Lambda,p}R^{2-\frac{4n+2}{p}}\norm{f_+}_{L^p(Q_R^-(P_0))}$ and the same constant: rescaling multiplies the source by $R^2$ and the volume by $R^{4n+2}$; for $a(x,v)$, where $n=1$ and $p>4$, the factor is $R^{2-\frac{6}{p}}$.
The estimate holds when $A=A(t,v)$ and $p>2n+1$, in every dimension $n$, and when $n=1$, $A=a(x,v)$ and $p>4$.
Both thresholds are optimal among those valid for all ellipticity ratios; for $A=A(t,v)$ the threshold $2n+1$ is the scaling threshold and is optimal for each fixed ellipticity ratio.

ideaClaims.text: For $A=A(t,v)$, integrating the adjoint kernel in position removes transport and leaves its velocity marginal, which the parabolic Aleksandrov estimate controls, while Fourier decay bounds the spatial supremum of the kernel on each interval $(T,2T)$ of elapsed time.

Interpolating the two bounds and summing over these intervals gives an $L^q$ bound for the space-time kernel when $1<q<1+\frac{1}{2n}$, and Duhamel's formula with Hölder's inequality turns it into the source range $p>2n+1$.

For $a(x,v)$ in dimension one, position serves as time while velocity stays away from zero; near zero velocity narrower intervals are used, and a Harnack comparison controls how their returning mass decreases with elapsed time, which gives every $p>4$.

The value $1+2n$ is the scaling lower bound; in cases (a) and (b) the exponent can go below $4n$, thanks respectively to the divergence-form structure and to the Fourier–Döblin cancellation estimate of the paper.

summaryClaims.text: Over a fixed time $L$, the Fourier transform of the kernel at any unit frequency $e$ has total variation at most $1-\delta$, a fixed improvement on the bound one that holds because the exponential has modulus one.

The constants $L>0$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$ depend only on $n,\lambda,\Lambda$, and the bound is uniform over the starting velocity $v\in\R^n$, the unit vector $e$, and every starting time $s$ for which the kernel is defined on $[s,s+L]$.

It is the unit-frequency contraction from which the Döblin–Fourier cancellation estimate is built: scaling gives the corresponding time for any non-zero frequency, and repeating the decrease on successive time intervals gives exponential decay.

The proof produces $L=L_0+4\rho^2$, with $L_0=1+\pi$ and a fixed $0<\rho<128^{-\frac{1}{3}}$, and $\delta=2(1-\varepsilon)\theta_0$, where $\varepsilon<\frac{1}{4}$ bounds a phase error and $\theta_0$ bounds from below the mass of a common minorant of two velocity marginals.

ideaClaims.text: Transport turns velocity into spatial displacement, and hence into Fourier phase: two families of velocity paths from the same starting velocity are arranged so that their waves acquire nearly opposite phases.

Cancellation needs more than opposite phases: the two velocity marginals must have a common positive lower bound, which the parabolic Harnack inequality supplies after both families evolve briefly in a fixed velocity ball.

Each family is kept in a narrow velocity tube around a prescribed path: the width of the tube leaves room for diffusion, so a barrier retains a positive mass, while the accumulated displacement stays close to the integral of the path.

On the portions supplied by the common minorant, the Fourier phases are close to two fixed values differing by $\pi$, so these portions cancel up to a small phase error, and the rest of the mass contributes at most its own total mass.

After reflecting position, this gives the following comparison for the full-space autonomous evolution St{\htmlClass{nt-autonomous-evolution}{\mathsf S}}_tSt​ with generator v∂X+a(X,v)∂vvv\partial_X+a(X,v)\partial_{vv}v∂X​+a(X,v)∂vv​:

for bounded Borel FFF [27, Lemma 8.7]. Here ttt is elapsed physical time. The constants and the Hölder exponent depend only on λ,Λ\lambda,\Lambdaλ,Λ. This kinetic comparison follows from the preliminary p=6p=6p=6 estimate.

proofHtml.fullHtml:
We apply Hölder continuity to a non-negative solution of Lu=0{\htmlClass{nt-kinetic-operator}{\mathcal L}}u=0Lu=0 in the original variables. It turns a positive value into a positive lower bound on a neighbourhood. At a fixed interior scale, if the solution has value k>0k>0k>0 and nearby supremum MMM, it stays above k2\frac{k}{2}2k​ on a kinetic cylinder of radius c(kM)1αc(\frac{k}{M})^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}c(Mk​)α1​. Its velocity width is of that order, its time length is the square of that order, and its position width is the cube.

A moving barrier carries this lower bound along a kinetic path, whose position derivative is its velocity [27, Lemma 9.3]. We also enlarge the cylinder as we move it. Doubling its radius costs only a fixed factor in the lower bound. Starting from radius ℓ\ellℓ, only order log⁡1ℓ\log\frac{1}{\ell}logℓ1​ doublings are needed to reach a fixed radius. The lower bound at a later point is therefore at least cℓβkc\ell^\beta kcℓβk, for a fixed β>0\beta>0β>0. This explains why propagation from the small neighbourhood remains useful.

The neighbourhood size still depends on MMM. Young’s inequality lets us bound the supremum on an inner cylinder by a multiple of the later value plus an arbitrarily small multiple of the supremum on a larger cylinder. We repeat this estimate on nested cylinders. The small factor makes the last supremum disappear in the limit, and is chosen to offset the cost of the shrinking gaps between cylinders.

summaryClaims.text: In suitable coordinates both coefficient classes reduce to an operator $\partial_\sigma+B(\sigma,y):D_y^2+b(y)\cdot\nabla_z$, with uniformly elliptic diffusion in the variables $y\in D$ and transport in the variables $z$ at a smooth, uniformly non-degenerate rate $b(y)$.
Since $B$ does not depend on $z$, each Fourier wave in $z$ evolves independently, and since the transport rate $b(y)$ changes with velocity, different velocity paths produce different phases.

For $A(t,v)$ the argument runs in the original time with $b(y)=y$ on $\R^n$; for $a(x,v)$ in dimension one position serves as time on a velocity interval of fixed non-zero sign, and the derivative of $b$ is bounded above and below by positive constants.

The same reduction is available for $A=A(\ell(t,x),v)$ with $\ell(t,x)=\alpha t+\beta\cdot x$, locally on bounded velocity regions where $\alpha+\beta\cdot v$ stays away from zero, since $\ell$ is then monotone along transport; a global estimate also requires combining these local bounds.

ideaClaims.text: Composing at an intermediate time $r$ writes $\widehat K^\xi_{s,t}(v,\cdot)$ as an integral of $\widehat K^\xi_{r,t}(v',\cdot)$ against the complex measure $\widehat K^\xi_{s,r}(v,\cdot)$, so the total variation is at most the product of the total variation of the first kernel and the supremum over the intermediate velocity $v'$ of that of the second.
The supremum over $v'$ is why the contraction must be uniform in the starting velocity: each interval starts from the velocities reached at the end of the previous one.

summaryClaims.text: For a piecewise $C^1$ path $\gamma$ on $[s,s+T]$ with $\abs{\gamma'}\leq H$, the kernel $K^{\gamma,\eta}$ killed outside the tube of radius $\eta$ around $\gamma$, started at the velocity $\gamma(s)$, keeps total mass at least $e^{-C(\eta^{-2}+H^2)T}$ at time $s+T$.
It is used with the two paths of the cancellation argument, and with a constant path to bound from below the mass of a Dirichlet velocity marginal in a ball.

ideaClaims.text: The tube leaves room for diffusion, and a barrier supported in the tube and moving with the path gives a lower bound for the mass that remains.
The barrier equals one at the centre of the tube, where the mass starts, so the lower bound is the exponential factor $e^{-C(\eta^{-2}+H^2)T}$ produced by its differential inequality.

proofHtml.fullHtml:
If instead v∉I‾v\notin\overline {\htmlClass{nt-velocity-intervals}{I}}v∈/I, the first arrival may be late. We apply the bound just proved from each arrival point, measuring time from that arrival, and integrate it against the first-arrival measure γ1{\htmlClass{nt-first-visit}{\gamma_1}}γ1​. summaryClaims.text: After reflection the operator is $\mathcal K=\partial_s+v\partial_X+a(X,v)\partial_{vv}$; on a bounded positive velocity interval separated from zero, dividing by $v$ makes $X$ the new time variable, transports the old time $s$, and leaves a diffusion coefficient $\frac{a(X,v)}{v}$ that does not depend on $s$, so the equation can be Fourier transformed in $s$.

For terminal data prescribed at a fixed $X$ and depending only on velocity, with zero data at the velocity endpoints, the solution does not depend on $s$ and solves $\partial_XV+\frac{a}{v}\partial_{vv}V=0$, which is uniformly parabolic after $X$ is reversed.
This is what allows the common-minorant argument to use the classical parabolic Harnack inequality in the variables position-as-time and velocity, with the old time integrated out.

ideaClaims.text: A stationary profile with $H(r^3x,rv)=r^\alpha H(x,v)$, flattened near the origin, has a source of size $O(\varepsilon^{\alpha-2})$ confined to a kinetic annulus of volume $O(\varepsilon^{4n})$, so its source norm is $O(\varepsilon^{\alpha-2+\frac{4n}{p}})$; the stationary profile alone does not contradict the time-dependent estimate, and after the modification that removes its initial height the source norm still tends to zero when $p<\frac{4n}{2-\alpha}$.

Because the stationary height sits in the initial data, a decaying super-solution is subtracted and a smooth approximation of the positive part is taken; this gives zero initial and lateral values while a fixed positive height remains at a fixed later time.

x.claim.critical-exponent-status.titleHtml: What is known about the critical kinetic exponent
x.claim.critical-exponent-status.statementHtml: Our result proves case (b), which reaches the optimal scaling lower bound, and gives the ellipticity-independent threshold 444 in case (c) when n=1n=1n=1 and A=A(x,v)A=A(x,v)A=A(x,v). Moreover, the autonomous counterexamples recorded in [27] exclude any p<4np<4np<4n independent of the ellipticity ratio in (c), for all n≥1n \ge 1n≥1, as explained in Section 8.5.

summaryClaims.text: The sharp kinetic Aleksandrov estimate proves case (b) of the conjecture, reaching the optimal scaling lower bound, and, for $n=1$ and $A=A(x,v)$, gives in case (c) the threshold $4$, independent of the ellipticity ratio.
The autonomous counterexamples recorded in the companion manuscript show that in case (c), for every $n\geq1$, no exponent $p<4n$ works independently of the ellipticity ratio.

In case (b), $A=A(t,v)$, the spatial smoothing that follows from the Fourier decay estimate reduces the problem to the parabolic setting in $(t,v)$, which permits the sharp kinetic range $p>1+2n$ down to the scaling obstruction; the optimal parabolic ellipticity-independent exponent $\max\{1+\frac{n}{2},n\}$ is always below this kinetic scaling lower bound.

For $n=1$ and $A(x,v)$ the companion manuscript also gives an ellipticity-dependent threshold strictly below four in case (c), whose optimal dependence on the ellipticity ratio remains open; in higher dimension and in the case $A(t,x,v)$, where the coefficients depend on all variables, it remains open to prove that $4n$ is the ellipticity-independent lower bound and to obtain the exact dependence on the ellipticity ratio below $4n$.

summaryClaims.text: At the endpoint $p=1+2n$ the strong Lebesgue form of the kinetic Aleksandrov estimate fails, even for constant coefficients.

We apply Krylov’s construction and Markov selection [21, 22] to the velocity operator, using a finite family of sphere charts. In local coordinates it has the form

aij∂ij+bk∂k,bk=−aijΓijk, a^{ij}\partial_{ij}+b^k{\htmlClass{nt-kinetic-boundary}{\partial_k}}, \qquad b^k=-a^{ij}\Gamma^k_{ij}, aij∂ij​+bk∂k​,bk=−aijΓijk​,
where Γijk\Gamma^k_{ij}Γijk​ are the Christoffel symbols. On the smaller chart domains, aaa is uniformly elliptic and bbb is bounded, with bounds depending only on the fixed atlas and ellipticity. No derivative of AAA occurs. The local martingale problems describe the same intrinsic operator on overlaps; localisation and compactness of the sphere give a global evolution, to which the selection theorem applies. This construction uses stochastic trajectories as an intermediate step. Smooth approximations produce velocity diffusions, and integrating X˙=V\dot X=VX˙=V gives their position. The joint distributions solve the full kinetic equation above. To pass to measurable AAA, one uses the parabolic Aleksandrov estimate, which controls occupation against the coefficient approximation errors, so the limiting distributions satisfy the weak equation. We use only the resulting evolution of measures.

summaryClaims.text: No Fourier decay tending to zero can hold uniformly over general coefficients with fixed ellipticity bounds: already in dimension one, no function $\eta(q)\to0$ bounds $\norm{\widehat u(1,N,\cdot)}_{L^1_v}$ by $\eta(\abs N)$ for every smooth coefficient with $\frac{1}{2}\leq a\leq\frac{3}{2}$ and every initial probability density $u(0,x,v)$, so no bound of the form of the Döblin–Fourier estimate, uniform also in the starting position, holds for such coefficients.

The example consists of smooth coefficients $a_N$ with $\frac{1}{2}\leq a_N\leq\frac{3}{2}$ and positive probability densities $u_N$, with normalised measure in $x$, whose Fourier mode at frequency $N$ has, at time $1$, an $L^1_v$ norm tending to $\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt\pi}>0$ as $N\to\infty$.
The Fourier method relies on the waves along the transported variable evolving independently, as for $A(t,v)$, where the coefficient does not depend on position.

ideaClaims.text: The coefficient $a_N$ depends on position through $\cos(Nx)$, at the frequency of the wave, so the waves in position are no longer decoupled.
The identity $(vq_N'-2q_N)''=vq_N'''$ makes the diffusion of the wave part of $a_Nu_N$ cancel the transport of the wave exactly, so the wave persists without decay.
The factor $N^{-3}$ in $q_N$ keeps the wave terms bounded by a multiple of the Gaussian, so that $a_N$ stays uniformly elliptic, while $\norm{q_N'''}_{L^1_v}$ stays bounded below.

x.claim.spherical-kernel-tools.titleHtml: Positivity, barriers and Harnack for the selected evolution
x.claim.spherical-kernel-tools.statementHtml: The selected evolution preserves positivity and mass. Stopping at velocity boundaries gives the Dirichlet kernels, and the stopped generator identity gives comparison with smooth barriers. Parabolic Harnack applies to nonnegative terminal-value solutions of the velocity evolution [35, Theorem 1.12 and its proof in Section 4]. It supplies the common lower bound (2.11) used below, without requiring classical regularity of ρt\rho_tρt​. All estimates are uniform over the choice of evolution; the invariant measure and generator refer to that choice.

summaryClaims.text: For every initial probability $\rho$ on $\T^n\times\mathbb S^{n-1}$, every velocity probability $\mu_s$ and all $s<t$, $\norm{\mathsf U_{s,t}\rho-\pi_t}_{\TV}\leq Ce^{-c\beta_\lambda(t-s)}$, where $\mu_t=\mu_sP_{s,t}$, $\pi_r=\dd x\otimes\mu_r$ and $\beta_\lambda=\min\{\lambda,\lambda^{-1}\}$, with constants depending only on $n,\frac{\Lambda}{\lambda}$.

The non-zero spatial modes make the position distribution uniform, and the zero-mode contraction makes velocity distributions from different initial data merge, so every evolved probability approaches $\dd x\otimes\mu_sP_{s,t}$, whatever $\mu_s$ is.

At $\abs k=1$ the Fourier rate is $\min\{\frac{1}{\lambda},\lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}\}\geq\beta_\lambda$, and the zero mode contracts at a rate proportional to $\lambda\geq\beta_\lambda$, so up to constants $\beta_\lambda=\min\{\lambda,\lambda^{-1}\}$ bounds both rates from below.

Thus vvv is the starting velocity, www the terminal velocity, and yyy the position displacement. We use measure notation because the argument does not require a density in velocity.

When a density in position exists, we write

summaryClaims.text: For $\bar v\neq0$ and $0<r\leq\frac23\abs{\bar v}$ it fixes three nested intervals $I_{\mathrm c}\subset I\subset I^*$ centred at $\bar v$: the estimate is wanted on $I_{\mathrm c}$, visits begin at $I$, and the equation is solved with zero values on $\partial I^*$. Every velocity in $I^*$ has the sign of $\bar v$.

In the coordinates $\sigma=\frac{X-X_e}{\bar vr^2}$ (rescaled position, the new time), $z=\frac{X-X_e-\bar v(s-s_e)}{r^3}$ and $y=\frac{v-\bar v}{r}$, one has $\dd s\dd X\dd v=r^6\dd\sigma\dd z\dd y$, and $\Ka$ applied to a function $h$ of the new variables equals $\frac{\abs v}{\abs{\bar v}r^2}$ times $\Lop_eh$, where $\Lop_e=\partial_\sigma+B_e(\sigma,y)\partial_{yy}+b_e(y)\partial_z$.
Because the coefficient is autonomous, $B_e$ does not depend on $z$: along a slice of fixed $\sigma$ the position is fixed while the old time varies.

The normalised coefficients satisfy $\frac35\lambda\leq B_e\leq3\Lambda$ and $\frac{9}{25}\leq b_e'\leq9$, so $\Lop_e$ is of type (I) with structural constants depending only on $\lambda$ and $\Lambda$, uniformly over the intervals used.
This is what lets the Fourier estimates of Sections 2 to 5 act on the autonomous equation, whose position-dependent coefficient prevents Fourier transformation in position.

summaryClaims.text: Let $\Gamma_e$ be the all-time Green measure of $\Ka$ from $e$ on the strip $(s_e,\infty)\times\R\times I^*$, killed when the velocity leaves $I^*$. It lives on $\{\sgn(\bar v)(X-X_e)>0\}$, and the change of variables of Lemma 8.2 carries $\abs v\,\Gamma_e$ to $\abs{\bar v}\,r^2$ times the Green measure $\widetilde\Gamma_e$ of $\Lop_e$.

summaryClaims.text: Alternating the evolution in $H_1=I^*\cap J_Q$ with the evolution in $H_2=J_Q\setminus\overline I$, each started from the other's exit measure on its interior boundary, defines measures $\gamma_k$ that record where and when the $k$th visit to $\overline I$ begins; a new visit is counted only after the mass has left $I^*$ and returned to $\overline I$.

ideaClaims.text: The quadratic velocity barrier bounds the mean time before leaving $I^*$ by $Cr^2$; by composition of killed kernels the mass still in $I^*$ then decays like $C\exp(-c\frac{t}{r^2})$.

Restarting from the mass remaining at time $t$ and applying Proposition 8.3 at each restart point gives the late part of the density the same exponential factor; on each time window only starting windows up to and including it contribute, with weights decaying geometrically in their distance, and Young's inequality for sequences sums the windows.

summaryClaims.text: For every starting point $P$ in the forward cylinder $\mathcal Q=\mathcal Q_R(Z_0)$ and every $1<q<\frac43$, the strip Green measure restricted to $\mathcal Q$ has a density with $\norm{G_P}_{L^q(\mathcal Q)}\leq C_{\lambda,\Lambda,q}\,R^{\frac6q-4}$.

For $|v_0|\leq8R$, the cores of the intervals with $\bar v=\pm\rho$ and $r=\frac\rho2$ cover each non-zero velocity with the same weight $\log\frac97$ in $\frac{\dd\rho}\rho$, and the bound of Lemma 8.8 is integrable in $\rho$ at zero exactly when $q<\frac43$.
For $|v_0|>8R$, a single interval with $\bar v=v_0$ and $r=4R$ covers the cylinder, and Proposition 8.3 gives the bound, in that case for every $1<q<\frac32$.

It is the output of the count of visits by time alone, and it yields the estimate for $p>4$, the last step of the order of argument displayed at the start of the subsection "Harnack improves the Aleksandrov estimate".

summaryClaims.text: For a Borel measurable $A:\R^{1+2d}\to\Sym_d$ with $\lambda I_d\leq A\leq\Lambda I_d$ almost everywhere and any $1\leq p<\infty$, every bounded admissible solution in $\Omega$ with Aleksandrov data $(p,C_{\mathrm A})$ is locally Hölder continuous with respect to the kinetic quasi-distance $d_{\kin}$, in the interior form stated next on compact subsets of $\Omega$, with $\alpha\in(0,1]$ and $C$ depending only on $d$, $\lambda$, $\Lambda$, $p$ and $C_{\mathrm A}$.

Quantitatively, under these hypotheses on $A$ and $u$ (bounded, admissible in $\Omega$ with data $(p,C_{\mathrm A})$, $1\leq p<\infty$, $C_{\mathrm A}<\infty$), if $R_0>0$ and $\overline{Q_{2R_0}^-(P)}\subset\Omega$ for every $P$ in a compact set $\mathcal C\subset\Omega$, then $\abs{u(P)-u(P')}$ is at most $C$ times the oscillation of $u$ on $\Omega_{R_0,\mathcal C}$, the union of the cylinders $Q^-_{2R_0}(P)$ with $P\in\mathcal C$, times $(\frac{d_{\kin}(P,P')}{R_0})^\alpha$, for all $P,P'\in\mathcal C$.

The equation enters only through the Aleksandrov hypothesis on smooth barriers, so the implication is valid for coefficients depending on all three variables; the companion proves the hypothesis only for its two coefficient classes.

The proof is the growth argument of Landis and Krylov–Safonov adapted to kinetic transport: positivity on most of a cylinder gives a lower bound on a smaller region, a moving barrier carries it to later points, a covering argument lowers the required fraction to any fixed one, and applying this to the solution and its negative reduces the oscillation.

No lower bound on $p$ is needed, and every $p<\infty$ serves: $p$ enters only through Lemma 9.2 and the choice of $\eta_*$, and all that is required there of the right-hand side of the hypothesis is that it tend to zero with the measure of the set $\{\psi>u\}$ on which the source is counted.

ideaClaims.text: The oscillation contraction contracts the oscillation by a fixed factor $q<1$ from $Q^-_R$ to $Q^-_{\vartheta R}$ at the same top point; iterating gives the factor $q^k$ on $Q^-_{\vartheta^kR}$.
The choice $\alpha=\min\{1,\frac{\log\frac1q}{\log\frac1\vartheta}\}$ makes $q\leq\vartheta^\alpha$, which turns this geometric decay into the power $(\frac\rho R)^\alpha$ at every radius.

Two distinct points at kinetic distance $\rho_*>0$ lie in the closed cylinder of radius $\rho_*$ whose top is the later point, so for $\rho_*<R_0$ the power decay at that centre controls their difference; for $\rho_*\geq R_0$ the oscillation bound suffices.

roleClaims.text: main-4 cites this theorem to say that its maximum principle at $p=6$ for autonomous coefficients is already strong enough to imply Hölder continuity for homogeneous solutions.

What main-4 takes is only this implication: the theorem needs the localised maximum principle for $\psi-u$ and $\psi+u$, for every smooth $\psi$, and accepts every $p<\infty$, so the exponent $p=6$ suffices.

main-4's next subsection applies the resulting Hölder continuity to a non-negative solution, turning a positive value into a positive lower bound on a neighbourhood, as the first step towards a Harnack inequality.

Corollary 9.10 (Hölder continuity for autonomous coefficients in one space dimension).

Let d=1d=1d=1, let a:R×R→[λ,Λ]a:\R\times\R\to[\lambda,\Lambda]a:R×R→[λ,Λ] be Borel measurable and let Ω⊆R3\Omega\subseteq\R^3Ω⊆R3 be open. Every bounded u∈C1,1,2(Ω)u\in C^{1,1,2}(\Omega)u∈C1,1,2(Ω) solving Lau=0\Pa u=0La​u=0 almost everywhere in Ω\OmegaΩ satisfies (9.7), with CCC and α\alphaα depending only on λ\lambdaλ and Λ\LambdaΛ.

summaryClaims.text: For $d=1$ and a Borel coefficient $a:\R\times\R\to[\lambda,\Lambda]$, every bounded $u\in C^{1,1,2}(\Omega)$ solving $\Pa u=0$ almost everywhere in $\Omega$ satisfies the Hölder estimate of Theorem 9.1, with $C$ and $\alpha$ depending only on $\lambda$ and $\Lambda$.
It combines the companion's one-dimensional autonomous maximum principle, used at the single exponent $p=6$, with Theorem 9.1.
For a Borel coefficient it is an a priori estimate for solutions of the stated classical regularity; no existence assertion is made.

summaryClaims.text: If $T_P=t_P-t_-\in[T_0,T_1]$ and a path $\bar x\in C^{1,1}([-T_0,T_P];\R^d)$ with $\abs{\ddot{\bar x}}\leq H$ almost everywhere ends at $P$, with its tube $\mathcal V$ contained in an open set $\mathcal T$, then a lower bound $u\geq\ell$ on $\mathcal V\cap\{t\leq t_-\}$ gives $u(P)\geq c_{\mathrm{prop}}\ell$, for every non-negative admissible supersolution $u$ in $\mathcal T$.

The path is a position curve $\bar x\in C^{1,1}$ with $\abs{\ddot{\bar x}}\leq H$ almost everywhere, whose derivative serves as the velocity: the tube consists of the points $(t_-+s,\bar x(s)+y,\dot{\bar x}(s)+V)$ with $-T_0\leq s\leq T_P$, $\abs y\leq\kappa_x$ and $\abs V\leq\kappa_v$, and it ends at $P=(t_P,\bar x(T_P),\dot{\bar x}(T_P))$.

The constant $c_{\mathrm{prop}}\in(0,1]$ depends only on $d$, $\lambda$, $\Lambda$ and the ratios $\frac{T_0}{T_1}$, $HT_1^{\frac12}$, $\frac{\kappa_v}{T_1^{\frac12}}$ and $\frac{\kappa_x}{T_1^{\frac32}}$, which express travel time, acceleration and tube widths in kinetic units; it does not depend on $p$ or $C_{\mathrm A}$.
The initial bound is assumed on a tube segment of positive duration $T_0$, because each comparison cylinder reaches slightly before its time interval.

The constant degenerates as $HT_1^{\frac12}$ grows and as $\kappa_vT_1^{-\frac12}$ and $\kappa_xT_1^{-\frac32}$ decrease; paths with prescribed endpoints are supplied by cubic Hermite paths, whose acceleration is bounded by the position mismatch over $T_P^2$ and the velocity mismatch over $T_P$.

ideaClaims.text: A Gaussian barrier centred on the path expands with velocity width proportional to $h^{\frac12}$ and position width proportional to $h^{\frac32}$.

With the damping factor $e^{-\Xi_h\sigma}$, the barrier satisfies $\PA\Psi\leq0$ almost everywhere on $\{0<\sigma\leq h\}$, for every admissible coefficient and every path acceleration up to $H$; in Step 4, if $\Psi\leq u$ on $\overline Q\cap\{\sigma\leq0\}$, then for the non-negative admissible supersolution $u$ both terms on the right of the comparison vanish, so the conclusion depends on ellipticity and the path geometry but not on $p$ or $C_{\mathrm A}$.

Comparison is made on short blocks; on each, the barrier's positive set stays inside a cylinder of radius a fixed multiple of $h^{\frac12}$ topped at the next path point, away from its kinetic boundary, and the barrier's height is reduced so that it fits below the preceding one.
The number of blocks is at most $n_*=\lceil\frac{T_1}{h_*}\rceil$, so the fixed loss $\gamma$ per block gives the constant $c_{\mathrm{prop}}=\gamma^{n_*}$.

titleClaim.text: Path-centred coordinates and a smooth path

summaryClaims.text: The proof works in path-centred coordinates $Z=(y,V)$, with a matrix for transport from velocity to position, one inserting diffusion in velocity, and the kinetic scaling with weights $h^{\frac32}$ and $h^{\frac12}$; the path is first mollified, at the price of halving $\kappa_x$ and $\kappa_v$, so that the barrier is smooth.

We construct the Gaussian in coordinates centred on the path. The matrix J\mathsf JJ describes transport from velocity to position, and V\mathsf VV inserts diffusion in velocity. Their covariance matrix, computed in Step 1, determines the Gaussian. At each step we start with the same rescaled profile and a smaller amplitude, using a time cutoff to make the comparison smooth. titleClaim.text: Path-centred coordinates and a smooth path

summaryClaims.text: The proof works in path-centred coordinates $Z=(y,V)$, with a matrix for transport from velocity to position, one inserting diffusion in velocity, and the kinetic scaling with weights $h^{\frac32}$ and $h^{\frac12}$; the path is first mollified, at the price of halving $\kappa_x$ and $\kappa_v$, so that the barrier is smooth.

Lemma 8.7 (A return-time comparison).

For every bounded non-negative Borel function FFF on R2\R^2R2,

StF(X,v)≤Cλ,ΛSsF(X,v),2t≤s≤3t,∣v∣≤t.(8.25) \mathsf S_tF(X,v)\leq C_{\lambda,\Lambda}\mathsf S_sF(X,v), \qquad 2t\leq s\leq3t,\quad |v|\leq\sqrt t. \tag{8.25} St​F(X,v)≤Cλ,Λ​Ss​F(X,v),2t≤s≤3t,∣v∣≤t​.(8.25)

summaryClaims.text: For every bounded non-negative Borel function $F$ on $\R^2$, the full-space evolution of $F$ at elapsed time $t$, evaluated at $(X,v)$, is at most $C_{\lambda,\Lambda}$ times its value at the same point at any time $s$ with $2t\leq s\leq3t$, provided $|v|\leq\sqrt t$.
The evolution is the positive full-space evolution with generator $v\partial_X+a(X,v)\partial_{vv}$, the increasing limit of the strip kernels on $(-M,M)$, which has mass one.

For the indicator of a velocity interval, the evolved function is the mass in that interval at time $t$; the comparison bounds it by a fixed multiple of its value at any time in $[2t,3t]$, so that averaging turns a time-integrated occupation bound into a bound at time $t$.

It is a kinetic Harnack-type comparison that controls returns in the original variables; its proof uses the Hölder theorem, made available by the preliminary $p=6$ estimate. It is used only for the full-space evolution: a kernel killed on a velocity interval of one sign cannot in general return to the same position later.

ideaClaims.text: Hölder continuity turns a positive value $u(z)$ into the lower bound $u\geq\frac12u(z)$ on a cylinder of radius $\ell=ch(\frac{u(z)}{M_b})^{\frac1\alpha}$, where $M_b$ is a nearby supremum.

Propagation along kinetic paths, doubling the radius at each step, carries a lower bound $k$ on a cylinder of radius $\ell$ to a later point with loss only $c\ell^\beta$: each doubling costs a fixed factor and about $\log\frac1\ell$ doublings are needed.
The resulting inequality still involves the supremum on a larger box; Young's inequality and iteration over nested boxes remove it.

ideaClaims.text: The barrier $\psi_r(v)=\sqrt{r^2+v^2}$ bounds the time integral of the mass in $\{|v|\leq3r\}$ up to time $T$ by $Cr\sqrt T$; averaging the comparison of Lemma 8.7 over $s\in[2t,3t]$ converts this, for starting velocities with $|v_e|\leq3r$, into the bound $C\frac r{\sqrt t}$ at each time $t\geq9r^2$.

The quadratic barrier then converts mass present into visits beginning: the visits beginning in a window of length $r^2$ are bounded by the mass in $I^*$ at its end plus $r^{-2}$ times its time integral over the window, with no constant added per window; for a start in $\overline I$ this gives $C(1+j)^{-\frac12}$ for the $j$th window.

Averaging over the first-arrival time and Young's inequality give $\sum_jm_j^q\leq C_q(1+\frac Rr)^{2-q}$ for $1<q<2$, on an observation interval of length at most $R^2$, which the power bound of Corollary 8.4 turns into the density bound.

Proof.

We justify the use of the singular barrier first. We convolve only in position, with a non-negative smooth approximate identity ηδ\eta_\deltaηδ​, and put Φδ=ηδ∗XΦ\Phi_\delta=\eta_\delta*_X\PhiΦδ​=ηδ​∗X​Φ. Appendix B verifies that the derivatives of Φ\PhiΦ have no distribution supported at the origin. The bound

∣Φvv(X,v)∣≤C∣X∣α−23 |\Phi_{vv}(X,v)|\leq C|X|^{\frac{\alpha-2}{3}} ∣Φvv​(X,v)∣≤C∣X∣3α−2​
is locally integrable in XXX. Thus Φδ\Phi_\deltaΦδ​ is smooth in position and twice continuously differentiable in velocity, including at v=0v=0v=0. Since (8.33) holds for every scalar bbb, we may hold b=a(X,v)b=a(X,v)b=a(X,v) fixed while convolving the shifted barrier. This gives
L[Φδ(X−Y,v)]≥c(ηδ∗Xρ−γ)(X−Y,v). L[\Phi_\delta(X-Y,v)] \geq c(\eta_\delta*_X\rho^{-\gamma})(X-Y,v). L[Φδ​(X−Y,v)]≥c(ηδ​∗X​ρ−γ)(X−Y,v).
Neither a derivative of aaa nor a transport error appears.

c E∫0Tρ(Xs−Y,Vs)−γ ds≤EΦ(XT−Y,VT)−Φ(X−Y,v)≤CMTα2. \begin{aligned} c\,\mathbb E\int_0^T\rho(X_s-Y,V_s)^{-\gamma}\dd s &\leq \mathbb E\Phi(X_T-Y,V_T)-\Phi(X-Y,v)\\ &\leq C_M T^{\frac\alpha2}. \end{aligned} cE∫0T​ρ(Xs​−Y,Vs​)−γds​≤EΦ(XT​−Y,VT​)−Φ(X−Y,v)≤CM​T2α​.​

Proposition 8.10 (A homogeneous Bellman barrier).

There is β∗=β∗(Λλ)∈[2,3)\beta_*=\beta_*(\frac\Lambda\lambda)\in[2,3)β∗​=β∗​(λΛ​)∈[2,3) such that, for every β∗−2<α<1\beta_*-2<\alpha<1β∗​−2<α<1, there are a function Φ∈C2(R2∖{0})\Phi\in C^2(\R^2\setminus\{0\})Φ∈C2(R2∖{0}) and a constant c>0c>0c>0 satisfying

Φ(r3X,rv)=rαΦ(X,v),ρ(X,v)=(X2+v6)16,vΦX+bΦvv≥cρα−2for every b∈[λ,Λ].(8.33) \begin{gathered} \Phi(r^3X,rv)=r^\alpha\Phi(X,v),\qquad \rho(X,v)=(X^2+v^6)^{\frac16},\\ v\Phi_X+b\Phi_{vv}\geq c\rho^{\alpha-2} \qquad\text{for every }b\in[\lambda,\Lambda]. \end{gathered} \tag{8.33} Φ(r3X,rv)=rαΦ(X,v),ρ(X,v)=(X2+v6)61​,vΦX​+bΦvv​≥cρα−2for every b∈[λ,Λ].​(8.33)

summaryClaims.text: There is $\beta_*=\beta_*(\frac\Lambda\lambda)\in[2,3)$ such that, for every $\beta_*-2<\alpha<1$, some $\Phi\in C^2(\R^2\setminus\{0\})$ with $\Phi(r^3X,rv)=r^\alpha\Phi(X,v)$ and a constant $c>0$ satisfy $v\Phi_X+b\Phi_{vv}\geq c\rho^{\alpha-2}$ for every $b\in[\lambda,\Lambda]$, where $\rho(X,v)=(X^2+v^6)^{\frac16}$; the function and constants depend only on $\lambda,\Lambda,\alpha$.

One function serves every coefficient value in the ellipticity interval, and taking the least favourable coefficient gives the stationary Bellman inequality $v\Phi_X+\min_{\lambda\leq b\leq\Lambda}b\Phi_{vv}\geq c\rho^{\alpha-2}$; the barrier need not be positive.

Its purpose is to control occupation of a box of width $r^3$ in position and $r$ in velocity, information that the time-only count of visits loses at $q=\frac43$, where the power $4-3q$ in the velocity-scale sum becomes zero.

The strict inequality $\beta_*<3$ makes the range $\beta_*-2<\alpha<1$ non-empty; the rest of the argument fixes one admissible $\alpha$ and sets $\gamma=2-\alpha\in(1,2)$ and $\varepsilon=1-\alpha=\gamma-1>0$.

The barrier extends continuously by zero to the origin and satisfies $|\Phi(X,v)-\Phi(X',v')|\leq C(|X-X'|^{\frac\alpha3}+|v-v'|^\alpha)$; its derivatives carry no distribution at the origin, so the inequality holds distributionally on the whole plane.

ideaClaims.text: The barrier is obtained by duality: if no $\alpha$-homogeneous $\Phi$ made $v\Phi_X+b\Phi_{vv}$ strictly positive for every $b\in[\lambda,\Lambda]$, separation would supply a positive measure annihilating all these expressions.

We fix β∗−2<α<1\beta_*-2<\alpha<1β∗​−2<α<1 and put Σ={ρ=1}\Sigma=\{\rho=1\}Σ={ρ=1}. In the space C(Σ×[λ,Λ])C(\Sigma\times[\lambda,\Lambda])C(Σ×[λ,Λ]), we consider the linear subspace of functions

(z,b)⟼vΦX(z)+bΦvv(z),z=(X,v), (z,b)\longmapsto v\Phi_X(z)+b\Phi_{vv}(z),\qquad z=(X,v), (z,b)⟼vΦX​(z)+bΦvv​(z),z=(X,v),

summaryClaims.text: For every $P\in\mathcal Q$ and $1<q<\frac{4-\varepsilon}{3-\varepsilon}$, the Green measure $\Gamma_P^{J_Q}|_{\mathcal Q}$ has a density $G_P$ with $\norm{G_P}_{L^q(\mathcal Q)}\leq C_{\lambda,\Lambda,q,\alpha}R^{\frac6q-4}$.

It extends the range $q<\frac43$ of Proposition 8.9 beyond $\frac43$: at $q=\frac43$ the density belongs to strong $L^{\frac43}$, so the maximum principle includes strong $L^4$ sources, and nearby $q$ give $p>4-\varepsilon=3+\alpha$.
The range is exactly where the velocity-scale sum of the core estimates converges, and its upper endpoint is less than $\frac32$, as the local estimates require.
The barrier provides the additional position bound, while the Döblin argument still supplies the local density on each one-sign interval; neither bound alone gives the conclusion.

summaryClaims.text: For every $d\geq1$ and $1\leq p<4d$ there are fixed bounds $0<\lambda\leq\Lambda$, a fixed kinetic cylinder $Q$, an autonomous measurable $A(x,v)$ with $\lambda I_d\leq A\leq\Lambda I_d$ and smooth non-negative $U_j$ vanishing on the initial and lateral boundary of $Q$, with $\sup_QU_j\geq\frac14$ and $\norm{(\mathcal L_AU_j)_+}_{L^p(Q)}\to0$.
The same holds with smooth autonomous matrices $A_j$ with the same ellipticity bounds; the bounds may depend on $d$ and $p$ but not on $j$.

The construction excludes every $p<4d$ for a suitable fixed ellipticity ratio; it says nothing at $p=4d$ and does not exclude every $p<4d$ at each fixed ratio, so it is consistent with the improvement below four in Theorem 1.2.
A stationary singularity gives a stronger obstruction than a shrinking smooth bump.

ideaClaims.text: A positive function $H$ with $H(r^3x,rv)=r^\alpha H(x,v)$, $0<\alpha<1$, solves $A:D_v^2H=v\cdot\nabla_xH$ away from the origin and vanishes there, so $1-H$ has height one at the origin and vanishes on the boundary of $\{H<1\}$.

Flattening $1-H$ near the origin keeps its height and confines the source to $\{r^\alpha\leq H\leq2r^\alpha\}$, of volume at most $Cr^{4d}$, on which $\abs{D_vH}\leq Cr^{\alpha-1}$; the source norm is therefore at most $Cr^{\alpha-2+\frac{4d}{p}}$, which tends to zero once $\alpha>2-\frac{4d}{p}$, and for $p<4d$ such an $\alpha<1$ exists.
A decaying velocity barrier removes the initial data without increasing the positive source, over a time interval that does not depend on $r$.

roleClaims.text: main-4 cites this construction for a stationary profile: a positive $H$ vanishing only at the origin, homogeneous of degree $\alpha\in(0,1)$ under $(x,v)\mapsto(r^3x,rv)$, which solves the stationary equation away from the origin for a suitable autonomous uniformly elliptic field, and whose flattening confines the source to a kinetic annulus.

main-4 also takes from it the removal of the initial data, by subtracting a decaying supersolution and taking a smooth approximation of the positive part, with the time interval and the ellipticity bounds fixed as the flattening scale tends to zero.

From these main-4 concludes, as the companion does, that taking $\alpha$ close to one excludes every exponent below four times the dimension for a suitable ellipticity ratio, without asserting failure below that value for each fixed ratio.

summaryClaims.text: On a velocity strip $\mathscr S_H=(s_-,s_+)\times\R_X\times H$, unbounded in position, each starting point $e$ has a Green measure $\Gamma_e^H$ on the strip and an exit measure $\omega_e^H$ on its exit boundary (terminal face and velocity faces), linked by the Green identity $\phi(e)=\int\phi\dd\omega_e^H-\int\Ka\phi\dd\Gamma_e^H$.
The exit measure has mass one, and the Green measure has mass at most $\min\{s_+-s_e,\frac{(v_e-h_-)(h_+-v_e)}{2\lambda}\}$: the time available, or a quadratic velocity barrier.
Both measures lie in the cone $\{\abs{X-X_e}\leq V_H(s-s_e)\}$; on an interval where $v$ has one sign, position moves monotonically, at speeds between $v_H=\inf_H\abs v$ and $V_H=\sup_H\abs v$.

The Green measure increases with $s_+$ and with $H$, and the nested identity splits the evolution on $H_2$ into the evolution on $H_1\subseteq H_2$ followed by the evolution on $H_2$ restarted from the exit measure on $\partial H_1\cap H_2$. This is what lets later proofs count repeated returns to smaller velocity intervals.
Potentials of non-negative smooth compactly supported sources $F$ are smooth, non-negative, solve $\Ka W=-F$ and vanish continuously on the exit boundary. The proof is in Appendix A.

ideaClaims.text: The level is lowered from $1$ to $\delta$, $\delta^2,\dots$: at each level, cylinders nearly full of the superlevel set give positivity on their forward stacks by the forward-stack lemma, and the covering theorem forces the measure of the next superlevel set to grow, up to an error controlled by a radius threshold.
After finitely many levels some nearly full cylinder must have radius above the threshold; its cap can be joined to every point of the target cylinder by Lemma 9.3.

The order of choices matters: the number of levels is chosen from $\beta$, then the threshold small enough for the accumulated covering error; a smaller cap gives a weaker bound, but the chosen cap has radius bounded below.

summaryClaims.text: The Green measure $\Gamma_\mu^S$ is the time integral of the evolution kernel of $\Lop$ started from a finite positive measure $\mu$ of mass $M$; integrating a source against it gives the solution with zero terminal and velocity-boundary data.

In case (I), for every $1<q<\frac32$, the all-time measure $\Gamma_\mu^\infty$ is finite and has a density with $\norm{G_\mu^\infty}_{L^q((0,\infty)\times J\times\R)}\leq C_{\lambda,\Lambda,m,L_b,\abs J,q}\,M$.

ka.x.preliminary-p6.titleHtml: The preliminary Aleksandrov principle at p=6p=6p=6
statementHtml:
We now use the regularity implied by the preliminary estimate to improve the estimate itself. The order of the argument is

Aleksandrov at p=6 ⟹ Ho¨lder continuity and a kinetic Harnack comparison ⟹ decay of returns in elapsed time ⟹ Aleksandrov for every p>4. \begin{aligned} \text{Aleksandrov at }p=6 &\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{H\"older continuity and a kinetic Harnack comparison}\\ &\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{decay of returns in elapsed time}\\ &\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{Aleksandrov for every }p>4. \end{aligned} Aleksandrov at p=6​ ⟹ Ho¨lder continuity and a kinetic Harnack comparison ⟹ decay of returns in elapsed time ⟹ Aleksandrov for every p>4.​
The preceding estimates already give the starting point, a preliminary Aleksandrov principle at p=6p=6p=6. Indeed, at q=65q=\frac65q=56​, Lemma 8.6 bounds the density on a core of scale r≤CRr\leq CRr≤CR by CR56r16CR^{\frac56}r^{\frac16}CR65​r61​. The continuous covering (8.32) below therefore gives
CR56∫0CRr16 drr≤CR. CR^{\frac56}\int_0^{CR}r^{\frac16}\frac{\dd r}{r}\leq CR. CR65​∫0CR​r61​rdr​≤CR.
There is no mass at v=0v=0v=0 by Lemma 8.5; cylinders with ∣v0∣>8R|v_0|>8R∣v0​∣>8R are covered by a single interval in Proposition 8.3. Proposition 6.2 thus gives the localised maximum principle at p=6p=6p=6. Applied to ψ−u\psi-uψ−u and ψ+u\psi+uψ+u for a homogeneous solution, it verifies (9.6). We may consequently use the conditional Hölder theorem and propagation lemma of Section 9, with constants depending only on λ,Λ\lambda,\Lambdaλ,Λ. This uses only the preliminary estimate, before either improvement.

summaryClaims.text: At $q=\frac65$, Lemma 8.6 bounds the density on a core of scale $r\leq CR$ by $CR^{\frac56}r^{\frac16}$, and covering the velocities by cores in $\frac{\dd r}{r}$ gives a total bound $CR$.
Since there is no mass at $v=0$ (Lemma 8.5) and cylinders with $|v_0|>8R$ are covered by a single interval (Proposition 8.3), Proposition 6.2 gives the localised maximum principle at $p=6$.

roleClaims.text: The short paper follows the same order in its treatment of coefficients $a(x,v)$: velocity barriers bound the returns and give the maximum principle at $p=6$, hence Hölder continuity, and the resulting Harnack comparison improves the estimate to every $p>4$; it refers to Sections 8 and 9 of the companion manuscript for the detailed proofs.

Its preliminary estimate integrates the interval bounds in $\frac{\dd r}{r}$ and then uses Hölder's inequality against the source and comparison to obtain the maximum principle at $p=6$, which it notes is strong enough for Hölder continuity of homogeneous solutions.

A visit begins when velocity first reaches I‾\overline {\htmlClass{nt-velocity-intervals}{I}}I, and ends when it leaves I∗{\htmlClass{nt-velocity-intervals}{I^*}}I∗ or the observation time ends. After that departure, a new visit begins only when velocity reaches I‾\overline {\htmlClass{nt-velocity-intervals}{I}}I again. Motion across ∂I\partial {\htmlClass{nt-velocity-intervals}{I}}∂I while still inside I∗{\htmlClass{nt-velocity-intervals}{I^*}}I∗ is part of the same visit. If the starting velocity lies in I‾\overline {\htmlClass{nt-velocity-intervals}{I}}I, the first visit begins immediately. Otherwise, it begins at the first arrival in I‾\overline {\htmlClass{nt-velocity-intervals}{I}}I.

More precisely, for a Borel set EEE in time, position and velocity, γk(E){\htmlClass{nt-visit-measures}{\gamma_k}}(E)γk​(E) is the amount of mass whose kkkth visit begins in EEE. Krylov’s Markov selection supplies a choice of evolution consistent with composition in time. frequency-time-scale.definitionHtml: At frequency $\xi$, a spatial displacement of order $\abs\xi^{-1}$ changes the phase by order one. Diffusion changes velocity by order $h^{\frac{1}{2}}$ over a time interval of length $h$, so transport produces a relative displacement of order $h^{\frac{3}{2}}$. The corresponding time scale is therefore $h=\abs\xi^{-\frac{2}{3}}$.

fig.anim-position-as-time.titleHtml: Position as time: a level of position becomes a slice of the new time

captionHtml.html: While the velocity stays in I∗⊂(0,∞)I^*\subset(0,\infty)I∗⊂(0,∞), position increases, so each position level reached before exit is crossed exactly once and position can serve as time. With q=∣ξ∣q=\abs\xiq=∣ξ∣ and e=ξ∣ξ∣e=\frac{\xi}{\abs\xi}e=∣ξ∣ξ​, an excursion of length rrr on a great circle through vvv and eee changes e⋅we\cdot we⋅w by sin⁡r≈r\sin r\approx rsinr≈r at the equator but only by 1−cos⁡r≈r221-\cos r\approx\frac{r^2}21−cosr≈2r2​ at the pole; held for a time of order r2r^2r2, it builds a relative phase of order qr3qr^3qr3, respectively qr4qr^4qr4. For ∣ξ∣≥1\abs\xi\geq1∣ξ∣≥1 and a fixed 0<r0≤180<r_0\leq\frac180<r0​≤81​, the scale is r=min⁡{r0,rˉ0}r=\min\{r_0,\bar r_0\}r=min{r0​,rˉ0​}, where e=av+be=av+be=av+b with bbb orthogonal to vvv, and rˉ0\bar r_0rˉ0​ is the positive root of ∣ξ∣(∣b∣r3+∣a∣r4)=1\abs\xi(\abs br^3+\abs ar^4)=1∣ξ∣(∣b∣r3+∣a∣r4)=1.
In the uncapped, high-frequency regime the time scale r2r^2r2 is q−23q^{-\frac{2}{3}}q−32​ at the equator and q−12q^{-\frac{1}{2}}q−21​ at the pole, so on a common clock the equator finishes first.

chapters.titleHtml: Conclusion: the rate q12q^{\frac12}q21​
chapters.summaryHtml: Although the construction time depends on vvv, the contraction is taken at a common time and is uniform in vvv; the pole sets the rate q12q^{\frac{1}{2}}q21​, which is optimal.

captionHtml.html: On the core Ic{\htmlClass{nt-velocity-intervals}{I_{\mathrm c}}}Ic​ the Green density satisfies ∥GP,I∥Lqq≤Cqr6−4q∑jmjq\norm{{\htmlClass{nt-interval-green-density}{G_{P,I}}}}_{L^q}^q\leq C_q{\htmlClass{nt-interval-radius}{r}}^{6-4q}\sum_j{\htmlClass{nt-visit-counts}{m_j}}^q∥GP,I​∥Lqq​≤Cq​r6−4q∑j​mj​q for 1<q<321<q<\frac{3}{2}1<q<23​, where mj{\htmlClass{nt-visit-counts}{m_j}}mj​ counts, with their kernel weights, the visits beginning in the window Jj{\htmlClass{nt-time-windows}{J_j}}Jj​ of length r2{\htmlClass{nt-interval-radius}{r}}^2r2.

(a) The velocity barrier alone, on the fixed enlarged strip, gives ∑jmj≤Cr\sum_j{\htmlClass{nt-visit-counts}{m_j}}\leq\frac{C}{{\htmlClass{nt-interval-radius}{r}}}∑j​mj​≤rC​ over the whole observation interval and mj≤C{\htmlClass{nt-visit-counts}{m_j}}\leq Cmj​≤C on each interval of length r2{\htmlClass{nt-interval-radius}{r}}^2r2, hence ∑jmjq≤Cqr\sum_j{\htmlClass{nt-visit-counts}{m_j}}^q\leq\frac{C_q}{{\htmlClass{nt-interval-radius}{r}}}∑j​mj​q≤rCq​​ and ∥GP,I∥Lq≤Cqr5q−4\norm{{\htmlClass{nt-interval-green-density}{G_{P,I}}}}_{L^q}\leq C_q{\htmlClass{nt-interval-radius}{r}}^{\frac{5}{q}-4}∥GP,I​∥Lq​≤Cq​rq5​−4.

With the Harnack comparison, the quadratic barrier gives the decay mj≤C(1+j)−12{\htmlClass{nt-visit-counts}{m_j}}\leq C(1+j)^{-\frac{1}{2}}mj​≤C(1+j)−21​ for j≥1j\geq1j≥1, which lowers the sum to ∑jmjq≤Cqrq−2\sum_j{\htmlClass{nt-visit-counts}{m_j}}^q\leq C_q{\htmlClass{nt-interval-radius}{r}}^{q-2}∑j​mj​q≤Cq​rq−2 for 1<q<21<q<21<q<2 and improves the interval bound to ∥GP,I∥Lq≤Cqr4q−3\norm{{\htmlClass{nt-interval-green-density}{G_{P,I}}}}_{L^q}\leq C_q{\htmlClass{nt-interval-radius}{r}}^{\frac{4}{q}-3}∥GP,I​∥Lq​≤Cq​rq4​−3 for 1<q<321<q<\frac{3}{2}1<q<23​. The gain comes from controlling when visits begin, rather than only their total count.

(b) The interval bounds are integrated against  drr\frac{\dd {\htmlClass{nt-interval-radius}{r}}}{{\htmlClass{nt-interval-radius}{r}}}rdr​. At q=65q=\frac{6}{5}q=56​ the preliminary bound is Cr16C{\htmlClass{nt-interval-radius}{r}}^{\frac{1}{6}}Cr61​, which is integrable and gives the maximum principle at p=6p=6p=6; the improved bound is integrable precisely when q<43q<\frac{4}{3}q<34​, that is p=qq−1>4p=\frac{q}{q-1}>4p=q−1q​>4.

(c) main-4 records a further improvement: a homogeneous Bellman barrier in the companion manuscript gives the estimate for every p>p∗(κ)p>p_*({\htmlClass{nt-ellipticity-ratio}{\kappa}})p>p∗​(κ) with p∗(κ)=1+β∗(κ)∈[3,4)p_*({\htmlClass{nt-ellipticity-ratio}{\kappa}})=1+\beta_*({\htmlClass{nt-ellipticity-ratio}{\kappa}})\in[3,4)p∗​(κ)=1+β∗​(κ)∈[3,4), including p=4p=4p=4; neither optimality of p∗p_*p∗​ nor an estimate at p=p∗p=p_*p=p∗​ is claimed.
